nodes.name: Calocedrus (cypress) forest
nodes.desc: A stand of these conifers covers about 50 km2 of the park on limestone, and Wikipedia says most of the trees are thought to be 500 to 600 years old.

nodes.name: Hopea and other lowland trees
nodes.desc: Evergreen tropical wet forest on limestone below 800 m covers about three quarters of the park. Hopea is one of its listed trees, and the leaves and fruit of such trees feed primates and other forest animals.

nodes.name: Rattan palms
nodes.desc: Climbing palms of the forest understory. Wikipedia lists rattan among the park plants that are overharvested.

nodes.name: Understory ferns and herbs
nodes.desc: Ferns such as spleenwort and other low plants carpet the shaded limestone forest floor. Spleenwort is recorded in the diet of the saola.

nodes.name: Butterflies and moths
nodes.desc: The park has recorded 259 butterfly species. Caterpillars eat leaves and the adults are food for birds, bats and ants.

nodes.name: Brown mabuya skink
nodes.desc: A common forest-floor lizard that eats small invertebrates. GloBI records it eaten by the brown shrike, the common mock viper and the little egret.

nodes.name: Hatinh langur
nodes.desc: A leaf-eating monkey of limestone forest that sleeps in cliff crevices and caves. Wikipedia says the park holds the largest known population in the world.

nodes.name: Red-shanked douc
nodes.desc: A colourful leaf-eating monkey. Wikipedia says the park runs a semi-wild zone that protects primates such as the douc.

nodes.name: Stump-tailed macaque
nodes.desc: One of several macaques in the park. An omnivore that eats fruit, seeds and other plant matter, and also takes some small animals.

nodes.name: Giant muntjac
nodes.desc: A large forest deer listed in the park, a browser on leaves and fruit, and one of the hoofed animals bears are reported to kill.

nodes.name: Mainland serow
nodes.desc: A goat-antelope of steep, rocky forest that browses leaves and herbs. Wikipedia lists it in the park, and bears are reported to kill serow.

nodes.name: Saola
nodes.desc: A rare ox-like animal confined to the Annamite Range, listed in the park as possibly present. It feeds on leaves, including spleenwort, pulled into the mouth with a long tongue.

nodes.name: Great roundleaf bat
nodes.desc: A large cave-roosting bat recorded often in the area. Ten threatened bat species have been recorded in the park, and bats eat flying insects at night.

nodes.name: Asian weaver ant
nodes.desc: Builds leaf nests in the canopy and hunts other insects in large colonies.

nodes.name: Brown shrike
nodes.desc: A small predatory bird that eats insects and small lizards. GloBI records it eating the brown mabuya skink.

nodes.name: Common mock viper
nodes.desc: A small snake that hunts lizards, and GloBI records it eating the brown mabuya skink.

nodes.name: Asian black bear
nodes.desc: Wikipedia confirms the bear in the park. It is mostly a plant eater but also eats insects, grubs and carrion and kills hoofed animals such as muntjac and serow.

nodes.name: Monsoon rain
nodes.desc: Heavy seasonal rain keeps the wet evergreen forest growing and feeds the underground rivers of the karst.

nodes.name: Limestone karst and caves
nodes.desc: The park sits in one of the two largest karst regions on Earth. Cliffs, caves and thin limestone soils shape which plants grow and give langurs and bats places to roost.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light reaching the forest canopy and understory drives plant growth in the tropical forest.

nodes.name: Soil fungi and bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, dead wood and bat droppings, returning nutrients to the thin karst soil.
